summary.text: Statistics is the discipline of collecting, organizing, analyzing, interpreting and presenting data.
When data on every member of a population cannot be collected, statisticians use survey samples and experiment designs, and random sampling lets conclusions reasonably extend to the whole population.
Descriptive statistics summarize a sample, while inferential statistics draw conclusions from data subject to random variation.

facts.label: Type I error
facts.value: Rejecting a null hypothesis that is true: a false positive

items.prompt: A city cannot ask all of its residents about a new park. What lets answers from some residents reasonably extend to everyone?

options.label: Waiting until a census is possible

items.explain: When a census cannot be collected, random sampling assures that conclusions can reasonably extend from the sample to the whole population.

items.prompt: Researchers measure a group of plants, change how much water they get, then measure them again the same way. What kind of study is this?
items.explain: An experimental study involves manipulating the system and measuring again; an observational study involves no manipulation.

items.prompt: A pollster questions 1,000 voters to make statements about a whole country. Which method of data analysis is that?
items.explain: Inferential statistics draws conclusions about a population from a sample, unlike descriptive statistics, which summarize the sample.

items.prompt: A test says a medicine works, though in truth it does nothing. Which kind of error is that?
items.explain: A Type I error is when the null hypothesis is rejected though it is in fact true, a false positive.

items.prompt: A survey records each person's favourite colour. What kind of data is that?
items.explain: Data may be a numerical value (quantitative) or a label (qualitative).

items.prompt: An analyst reports weights in pounds while everyone believes they are in kilograms. What kind of error is that?
items.explain: Errors can be random (noise), systematic (bias), or other types such as a blunder, for example reporting incorrect units.
